name: Eczema
tagline: Itchy, dry skin. Moisturise. Manage triggers.

what_is_it.heading: Eczema in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Eczema (also called atopic dermatitis) is a long-term skin condition where the skin barrier doesn't hold moisture well and gets easily irritated. The result: dry, itchy, inflamed patches — sometimes flaring badly, sometimes calm.
paragraphs: Eczema usually starts in childhood — about 1 in 5 South African children have it. Many improve with age, though it can return at any point. Adult-onset eczema is also common. It often runs alongside asthma, hay fever, or food allergies — the 'atopic triad'.

Eczema is not contagious. It is not caused by being dirty or by poor hygiene. The skin barrier in eczema is just genetically different — more porous, more reactive. The good news: with daily moisturising and trigger management, most people keep it well controlled.

items.headline: 1 in 5
items.body: South African children have eczema. Many improve with age. Adult eczema is common too.

items.headline: Moisturiser wins
items.body: Daily moisturising — even when skin looks fine — is the single most powerful eczema treatment. Skip a few days and the flare comes back.

items.headline: Not contagious
items.body: You cannot catch eczema. It is not caused by dirt or hygiene. It is a genetic skin barrier issue, often with allergic component.

items.headline: Steroid creams work
items.body: Topical steroids during flares are safe when used correctly. They calm the inflammation so the skin can heal.

pull_quote.text: Most eczema is well controlled with two simple steps: moisturise twice a day every day, and use a steroid cream when flaring. The mistake most people make is stopping the moisturiser when the skin looks fine.

signs.heading: What eczema looks like
signs.lede: Eczema shows up in typical places and has typical patterns. The look can differ on different skin tones — on darker skin it can appear grey, purple, or darker brown rather than the textbook red.

items.title: Babies and young children
items.description: Cheeks, scalp, and outer arms and legs. Red (or darker, on Black skin), dry, often crusty patches. Very itchy — babies scratch even in their sleep.

items.title: Older children and adults
items.description: Skin folds — inside elbows, behind knees, wrists, neck, ankles. Patches of thickened, scaly, itchy skin. Hands and eyelids common in adults.

items.title: When to worry — infection
items.description: If patches become weepy, yellow-crusted, very painful, or spread fast — it may be infected. Needs clinic assessment for antibiotics or antiviral treatment.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Steroid creams will damage my skin.
items.fact: Used correctly for short courses during flares, topical steroids are safe and effective. Avoiding them causes more harm — chronic uncontrolled eczema thickens skin and causes infection.

items.myth: Eczema is caused by something in the diet.
items.fact: True food allergies do trigger eczema in some children — but most eczema is not food-driven. Avoid elimination diets without medical advice; they can cause real nutritional harm.

items.myth: If you scratch enough, you can scratch it out.
items.fact: Scratching damages the skin barrier further, releases more itch chemicals, and creates a vicious itch-scratch cycle. Cold compresses, moisturiser, and antihistamines help — scratching doesn't.

items.myth: Children always grow out of eczema.
items.fact: Many do, but many don't. Even those who 'grow out' can have flares as adults. Lifelong skin care habits — gentle cleansers, daily moisturiser — are worth building early.

prevention.heading: Daily habits that keep flares away
prevention.lede: Eczema management is mostly about daily skin care — small habits that prevent the next flare.

items.title: Moisturise twice a day, every day
items.description: Thick fragrance-free moisturiser within 3 minutes of bathing seals in water. Continue even when skin looks fine — this is what prevents the next flare.

items.title: Lukewarm short baths or showers
items.description: Hot water strips the skin. Use lukewarm water, fragrance-free wash (not regular soap), 5–10 minutes maximum. Pat dry — don't rub.

items.title: Know and avoid your triggers
items.description: Common triggers: heat and sweat, wool and synthetic fabrics, harsh soaps and detergents, stress, allergens (pets, dust). Keep a flare diary to spot yours.

items.title: Cool, calm bedroom
items.description: Heat and sweat worsen night-time itch. Keep the bedroom cool, use cotton sheets, and don't over-bundle children. Cooler is calmer.

action_steps.heading: What to do when it flares

items.title: Apply steroid cream for active flares
items.description: Available from clinics — usually hydrocortisone (mild) for face and babies, stronger for body. Use thinly on red patches twice a day until calm. Then stop.

items.title: Keep moisturising — even over the steroid
items.description: Apply moisturiser 30 minutes after the steroid, or at other times. The moisturiser supports healing — don't stop because you're using steroid.

items.title: Take an antihistamine for severe itch
items.description: Cetirizine or loratadine help with itch, especially at night. Available over the counter at any pharmacy. Particularly useful for children who scratch in their sleep.

items.title: If skin becomes weepy or infected — go to clinic
items.description: Yellow crusting, painful spreading, fever — may be a bacterial infection (staph) or eczema herpeticum (viral, more serious). Needs treatment quickly.

items.title: For severe or hard-to-control eczema
items.description: Government clinics can refer to a dermatologist. New treatments like dupilumab (biologic injection) have transformed severe eczema in recent years.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Most eczema is well managed at clinic level. Severe cases benefit from dermatology referral — available through the public system.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Free eczema assessment, moisturisers, and steroid creams
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required
